justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-sloping baseline across all three horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I anchored heavily on recent price action and short-term momentum, assuming relatively stable conditions with minimal overnight shock. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild continuation bias — markets in the context I was forecasting appeared to have modest upward drift built into near-term expectations. The 1-month estimate extends that drift further, incorporating a slightly more optimistic longer-run mean, while also accounting for the possibility that any near-term softness would partially recover by month-end. In all three cases, the point estimates are relatively close together, suggesting I did not expect a dramatic directional move over this period.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the expected behavior under almost any reasonable uncertainty model. At one day, the range is roughly 22 points wide, reflecting the typical intraday-to-overnight variability one might expect. By one week, the interval expands to about 42 points, capturing the compounding of daily volatility and sensitivity to macro data releases or sentiment shifts within the week. At one month, the interval stretches to roughly 86 points, acknowledging that a full month introduces earnings cycles, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, and trend reversals that are simply impossible to anticipate with precision.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden and significant macroeconomic surprises — an unexpected inflation print, a central bank policy pivot, or a sharp deterioration in credit or labor market data. On the upside, a surprisingly strong risk-on catalyst, such as a ceasefire in an ongoing geopolitical conflict or a better-than-expected earnings season, could drive prices well above the upper bound of the 1-month interval. On the downside, a liquidity event, a financial stability scare, or a significant geopolitical escalation could easily break through the lower bound.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions with relatively stable volatility. If realized volatility were to spike — as happens during market stress — the true distribution of outcomes would have fatter tails than my stated intervals imply. My stated 90% confidence intervals should therefore be understood as conditional on a relatively "normal" market environment, and tail events by definition remain underweighted in any such parametric framing.
